column2: and the sight of the cut, torn, broken and the united — thus one should arrange jugglery for the dismay of enemies.
Breaking of unbroken forces and gathering of the broken, frightening, striking at the gate, protecting the treasury, elephant work,
breaking the unbroken, joining friends, chariot work; scouting forest, direction and paths, marking provisions and rear-support,
following and retreating, accomplishing quick tasks, following the wretched, striking at the tips and the rear;
horse work and the infantry's constant bearing of weapons, clearing the camp, roads and the like, and settling work.
Ground for infantry free of thick stumps, anthills, trees, bushes and thorns, with space to retreat, not too uneven, is held good;
for horses ground with few trees and stones, with hills easily crossed, firm, free of gravel and mud and with room to retreat;
for chariots ground without stumps, trees or ditches, free of mud, free of trees to be crushed or cut, and creepers and mud;
for elephants uneven ground, with streams and hills not easily approached. Receiving the broken forces from the chest and the like
is called the reserve (pratigraha), capable of the king's other works; a formation empty of it appears as if broken.
The wise one desiring victory should not fight without a reserve. Where the king is, there is the treasury; kingship depends on the treasury;
therefore he should give to the warriors; it is not proper to give little. A lakh of wealth for killing a king; half that for harassing his son;
likewise for killing a commander, for crushing elephants and the like. Or warriors should fight horse against horse, chariot, elephant:
so that there is no obstruction in the turning back of exercise; they should fight without mixing; mixing brings confusion.
In great confused fights they should take refuge with an elephant. Three men should be opponents for a horse;
thus three horses should be arranged for an elephant; and fifteen men should be foot-guards;
thus the arrangement for an elephant and for a chariot is prescribed. An "anika" is to be known: nine elephants are to be arranged;
and the gap of the anika is said to be fivefold; so by division of the anika one should establish the riches of formations.
The chest, flanks and wings are these arrangements: chest, flanks and wings, middle, back, reserve,
and the tips — by those who know the science of formations a formation is called seven-limbed. Chest, flanks and wings are this formation with reserve;
this is of the teacher and of Shukra, avoided with the flanks. The commanders should stand surrounded by heroic men;
they should fight without division and protect each other. In the middle formation the army is thin; the fighting material is at the rear.
Battle has the leader as its life; when the leader is struck, it is struck. In the chest one should station fierce elephants, chariots on the flanks,
and horses on the wings; the formation is declared a middle-breaker. In the middle a horse-force, chariot-force on the flanks,
and elephant-force on the wings — this is remembered as the inner-breaker. In place of chariots one should give horses, infantry in place of horses;
in absence of chariots one should give elephants everywhere in the formation. If there is a preponderance of the staff, it is called "abadha";
the circle, the uncompact "bhoga," those "danda" in many ways — hear: a staff is a transverse movement; the bhoga is another movement;
the mandala is all-round movement; the asamhata is separate movement; pradara, dridhaka, asahya, chapa and kukshi;
pratishtha and supratishtha, shyena, vijaya and sanjaya; vishala, vijaya, suchi, sthuna, karna and chamumukha;
sarpasya and valaya — staff and divisions of staff are hard to conquer. Atikranta and pratikranta by the flanks and one flank or wing;
atikranta by two wings; three others are the reverse of that. By wings and chest, atikranta; pratishtha is another reversal;
sthunapaksha, dhanuhpaksha, dvisthuna, upward-moving staff, dviguna; atikrantapaksha is another reversal;
dvi-chatur-danda — these are to be known by their marks in order. Gomutrika, ahisancari, shakata and makara likewise
are declared the divisions of bhoga; so too pariplavanga; the staff and wings: yugarasya; shakata is the reverse;
makara is the mixed; the rest by rows of elephants. The two divisions of the mandala formation are sarvatobhadra and durjaya;
the second is eight-forced, the first all-faced; ardhachandraka, urdhvanga, and varieties of vajra from the compact;
and karkata-shringi, kakapada and godhika are to be known for three- and four-fold armies by difference of shape.
For the staff there are seventeen formations, two for the circle, six for the uncompact, five for the bhoga in battle.
Having struck with one of wings and the rest, one should surround with the rest; or having struck with the chest, one should enclose with the two tips;
having assailed the enemy's tips with the wings, because of lack of reserve, one should strike the rear with the tips and press with the chest.
Where the force is thin, where broken, and where occupied by others, there one should strike the enemy's force and reinforce one's own;
one should press the strong by a double-strong and the thin by a strong; one should split the compact force with fierce elephant-forces.
The staff formation may be with flanks, wings and chest, in operation; there the application of the staff one should show by the fourth position.
Surpassed by staff and equal wings it is remembered as "dridha"; surpassed by wings and flanks it would be "pradaraka";
by the flanks the formation advanced is remembered as "asahya"; with flanks and wings below, and the chest, the "kanta" and "khataka."
Two staffs are called valaya, and kanta and khataka; the four-valaya is unconquerable, crusher of the enemy's force.
With flanks, wings and chest the bhoga turns the field: serpent-moving, gomutrika, shakata with cart shape;
the reverse is called "amara," crusher of all enemies. The mandala is the merging of flanks, wings and chest;
wheel, lotus and the rest are the varieties of the mandala. So too sarvatobhadra, vajra-like, shreshtha-kaka-like,
half-moon, shringata, and achala by name and form. Formations should be made at ease to ward off the enemies' force.
Agni said: Rama, having killed Ravana, reached Ayodhya, twice-born; by the policy told by Rama Lakshmana earlier killed Indrajit.
Six high, eight-boned, seven oily, nine clean, ten lotus-like, ten spread, with banyan-like proportions,
fourteen paired equal, sixteen imperishable is praised; joined with dharma, wealth and desire, dharma is held as one more.
Eyes without pupils... white teeth, two white things, deep, three-eared, navel, and one sattva — the triad is remembered:
freedom from envy, compassion, forbearance, auspicious conduct, purity, desirelessness, non-meanness, effortlessness and valor.
A man with three marks, three long parts, in testicles and arms; one who by splendor, fame and prosperity pervades directions, places, castes and groups
is a three-pervader, a man with three folds; three folds on the belly — hear of the three-bent man:
one who bows to gods, Brahmins and teachers, knower of times of dharma, wealth and desire, is called a knower of three times.
Chest, forehead and face broad, with lines; both hands and both feet joined with banner, umbrella and the like;
fingers, heart, back and waist praised as four-equal; ninety-six fingers in height by four cubits measure;
four teeth moon-bright; I tell you the four blacks: pupils of the eyes, brows, beard and hair black likewise;
in nose, mouth, sweat, and armpits a scent like feces; short organ, neck and shanks, and short veda...
delicate finger-joints, nails, hair, teeth and skin; jaws, eyes and forehead, nose long, between the breasts;
chest, armpits, nails, nose, raised face, nape; glossy skin, hair and teeth; body-hair, gaze, nails and speech;
of knees and thighs and back; two bamboos, of hands and nose; eyes, nostrils, ears, organ, anus and mouth clean;
tongue, lips, palate, eyes, hands, feet and nails, tip of organ and face — these ten of embodied beings are praised as lotus-like.
Hands and feet, face, neck, ears, heart, head, forehead, belly, back — ten large ones are honored.
For one with arms stretched, the span between the tips of the two middle fingers equals his height — banyan-measured.
Feet, ankles, buttocks, sides, groins, testicles, breasts, ears, lips, thighs, shanks, hands, arms and eyes —
fourteen pairs equal: such is the man in general. One who sees the fourteen knowledges with two eyes, with sixteen eyes —
rough, with spread veins, inauspicious, fleshless, foul-smelling, the reverse of what is praised — with a gracious look.
A fortunate man's speech is sweet, gait like an elephant in rut; hair from one pore; in fear protection again and again.
Navel turning to the right, private part like a pipal leaf, ankles concealed, navel a thumb in size at the middle;
belly not hanging, body-hair not rough — such is not good. One not named after stars, trees or rivers, not always fond of quarrel,
not greedy, not foul-spoken, is auspicious, honored by gods and the rest; with cheeks like madhuka flowers, not veiny, not hairy.
